name: Recon Desk

cover.alt: Illustration of two export sheets, matched by record key, with a changed amount marked for review.

summary: Compare CSV and Excel exports, then review bank-to-books matches. File processing stays in the browser.
ownership: I built the application end to end.
sections: Comparison
Key-based comparison supports composite identities, duplicate-key reporting, exact decimal tolerances and reusable profiles. Results export as CSV, JSON or a workbook of text cells.
Reconciliation
Candidate matches use amounts, dates and references. Users confirm or reject suggestions, handle unmatched items and review balances before explicitly completing a reconciliation.
Monthly accounting

Remaining items are classified as outstanding payments, deposits in transit, bank entries to record or errors to investigate. Source balances are validated, and unresolved items carry into the next period with their history, so an item that clears next month is not counted again as new movement.
Processing and sessions

Workers hold the full datasets while the interface requests bounded result pages. Reconciliation decisions can be saved in IndexedDB or exported as a session backup. Source files are reread when restoring a session.
Decision identity and completion

Review events identify transactions by side, source-file fingerprint and record number. Replacing a source file cannot attach old decisions to different transactions. Completion records the files, mappings, rules and balances it was reviewed against; a later event or changed basis withdraws that completion.
images: Changed values, record counts and export options.
Candidate bank and books transactions with explicit confirm and reject actions.

home.label: Independent project · browser tool
home.tagline: Compare exports and review bank-to-books matches in your browser.
highlights: Leading zeros are preserved, and duplicate keys are flagged for review.
Reuse a saved profile for the next export.
Download CSV, JSON or XLSX with values stored as text cells.
notes: Recurring exports make meaningful changes hard to spot. Row order and formatting can add noise. I built the comparison and reconciliation tool around reusable rules.
Match by identity, use exact decimal operations, and keep file processing in workers. Duplicate keys are reported as ambiguous instead of guessed.
This local example compares three sample records and one amount field. The full tool supports CSV/XLSX input, saved profiles, reconciliation and export. Legacy .xls is excluded.

decision.label: Recon Desk
decision.title: Don’t guess when keys repeat.
decision.implementation: Duplicate keys are reported rather than matched arbitrarily. Composite keys use ordered parts, and identifiers retain leading zeros.
decision.boundary: The comparison excludes ambiguous keys from matching on both sides.

problem: Recurring exports arrive reordered, reformatted and sometimes with duplicate identifiers, so meaningful changes are hard to see. Bank reconciliation adds different dates, references, sign conventions, grouped payouts and items that clear in a later month. A row-by-row diff or an amount-only match misclassifies these cases.
challenges: Large files without a frozen interface
Parsing, comparing and exporting can involve millions of fields, and handing a whole result to React still costs copying and rendering.
Workers keep the full data and results. The interface requests typed, bounded pages and renders virtualised rows.
More protocol and lifecycle code. Workers still hold whole files in memory; this is not a streaming engine.
Avoiding misleading matches
Same-amount transactions compete, and debit and credit labels mean different things in bank and books exports.
Normalise to explicit money in and out, require exact signed amounts within a declared date window, group competing candidates and leave confirmation to the reviewer.
More manual review when candidates compete. A candidate budget bounds the search and reports it as incomplete rather than as “no match”.
Recoverable work without a server
Cancelling a worker, reloading the page or a second open tab could lose or overwrite review decisions.
Keep ordered decisions outside the workers, replay them against source-file fingerprints, validate versioned backups and check revisions inside one IndexedDB transaction.
Original files must be supplied again after a reload. Browser saving is not a cloud backup.

Unit test run while preparing the project notes. Not a coverage figure.

candidate pairs suggested in 0.8–1.0 s

per file, compared, scrolled and exported in the browser
Approximate size, one recorded run in Chrome on an M4 with 16 GiB. Not a capacity promise for every device.
limits: No application server, accounts, bank feeds or accounting-system writes. Suggestions are never confirmed automatically, and reconciliation is labelled experimental in the tool.
result: A publicly hosted tool with two local-file workflows: comparing exports and reconciling a bank statement against books. Review decisions survive reloads, unresolved items carry into the next month, and reports download in several formats.

demonstration.title: Review a suggested match
demonstration.intro: Try two competing candidates for one bank entry. Confirm one, reject the suggestion, or leave it unresolved. The review decision changes the outcome.
demonstration.boundary: Interactive explanation with synthetic records. This illustrates manual review, not the full matching engine, date rules or candidate budget.

labels.sample: Synthetic sample · same amount, competing candidates
labels.idleNote: Equal amounts alone cannot decide which record belongs to this bank entry.
labels.pickedNote: Selecting a candidate does not confirm it. The reviewer makes that decision explicitly.
labels.matchedNote: The chosen candidate is confirmed. The competing candidate remains unpaired.
labels.unmatchedNote: No candidate is confirmed. The entry remains available for investigation and classification.

name: Internal Operations Platform
indexSummary: Order tracking and offline survey work. I built most of the frontend and the offline functionality on both frontend and backend.

cover.alt: Illustration of a site-survey clipboard and phone, with saved measurements queued for the server.

summary: One platform connecting orders, site surveys, production, dispatch and installation. My work spans the frontend and selected backend services, including the complete offline implementation.
ownership: I owned most frontend development and built the offline functionality across both frontend and backend. I worked in an existing team codebase.
sections: Field workflows
Built survey grids, unit measurement panels, photo and deviation handling, order and work-order selection, scanning flows and mobile operator screens.
Prepared offline work

Prepared grids and unit details are stored locally. An IndexedDB-backed queue retains edits and photos, sequences saves per unit and reconciles with the server after reconnecting. Saving on the device is distinct from server confirmation and survey completion.
Scanning and the installable app

Production and dispatch screens resolve component QR or serial codes against a scoped manifest and stage valid pieces with counts before submission. The app installs as a PWA with a cached shell, update prompts the user controls and a pending-sync indicator.
Backend contributions

Work included bulk offline reads and saves, activity and comments APIs, session authentication changes, query optimisations and concurrency fixes. The backend uses Fastify, TypeBox, Drizzle and PostgreSQL.
Photos before the batch

Offline photo references are resolved to uploaded URLs before a bulk save is sent. Per-unit mutation scopes keep dependent edits in order, so a batch contains at most one save per unit. Each save settles with its own result; accepted server data replaces the optimistic view, while rejected saves roll back and refetch.
images: Order-level progress and component summaries, using dummy records.
Survey, sales-order and handover tasks within the same order.
A selected unit opens measurement, remarks, photo and deviation controls.
A pending-sync badge and local-save message distinguish queued work from server confirmation.

decision.label: Offline field work
decision.title: Saved locally is not synced.
decision.implementation: Prepared reads and pending edits live in IndexedDB. Saves are sequenced per unit, with at most three concurrent sync operations.
decision.boundary: The server remains authoritative. Local saving, server confirmation and survey completion are separate states.

problem: Office, factory and site teams work on the same orders at different levels: the order, each unit and each component. Surveyors also work where connectivity is unreliable. The platform keeps order-level coordination consistent with unit and component work, from site survey through installation and handover.
challenges: One invalid scan, one failed batch
A single invalid component could make the backend reject a whole batch of scans.
Scoped scan manifests and local checks reject unknown, duplicate, already-processed and not-yet-produced components before they enter the batch.
Locally cached eligibility can become stale, so the backend still revalidates every submission.
Reconnect bursts

A reconnect resumed every queued save at once, one per unit. Requests waited in the browser's connection queue with their timeouts already running, so saves timed out while the server was answering and the stuck-save rule discarded them. On the backend, each save held two pool connections, so about 30 concurrent saves could stall a 30-connection pool.

A shared limit of three in-flight saves, below the handful of connections a browser keeps per host, so each timeout starts only when its request can actually go out. Each save now reads before its transaction and holds one connection, and the order refreshes once per burst instead of after every save.
Three was set from the browser's connection limit, not from load testing. Bounded concurrency can drain the queue more slowly than unrestricted parallel requests.
Preparing work for offline use
Preparing grids and each unit’s details produced many separate requests.
Bulk grid reads and cursor-paginated unit-detail preparation, supported by matching backend changes.
Bulk payloads still grow with the size of the project hierarchy.
limits: Offline support covers prepared survey and installation work, not the whole application. The server remains authoritative for permissions, workflow eligibility and confirmed records.
result: Surveyors keep recording measurements, photos and installation progress without a connection, and queued work syncs in order on reconnect. Reconnect traffic is bounded, offline preparation uses batched reads instead of per-unit requests, and invalid scans are rejected on the device before a batch is sent. No before-and-after measurement of timeouts or lost saves has been taken yet.

name: Sales CRM & Browser Telephony
indexSummary: Browser calls, quotations and sales workflows built on Frappe CRM, with a handoff to the operations platform.

cover.alt: Illustration of a browser-call headset linking an agent and customer, beside a quotation and contact card.

summary: Company-specific development on an existing Frappe CRM: browser calling, lead qualification, quotation reviews, permissions and a controlled handoff into operations.
ownership: I owned most of the custom frontend and Python backend development. The Frappe CRM platform was already installed when I joined.
images: Sample lead with separate business stage and engagement fields, plus inbound and outbound call activity.
Sample leads grouped by configured business stage in the Frappe CRM Kanban view.
Sample lead records and stage, source and owner filters in the Frappe CRM list view.
sections: Sales workflows and access

Implemented separate business-stage and engagement-state rules, required-field validation, call dispositions and hierarchy-aware permissions. Visibility and write access are enforced through backend checks as well as the interface.
Browser telephony

Built the Exotel browser calling interface and backend integration, including inbound and outbound calls, wrap-up notes, dispositions and recording playback. Call correlation, early-event buffering, tab ownership and scheduled reconciliation handle provider and browser lifecycle issues. Provider outcomes determine whether the customer answered; the browser connecting alone is not sufficient. An early invitation is accepted as the outbound agent leg only when its call identifier exactly matches the successful dial response.
Quotation review and revision

Implemented quotation requests, uploads, review, revision and acceptance. Revisions supersede the earlier request and create a linked successor, preserving prior files and feedback. Accepted commercial values synchronise back to the lead, with permissions restricting who can submit and review.
Website intake and attribution

Built the Python lead-intake API used by the public website, including phone normalisation, matching, eligible reactivation and campaign attribution. Existing closed records are not silently reopened.
Operations handoff

Built a project-creation action with permission and data checks, expiring signed quote-file links and retries after failure. The handoff is marked complete only when both the project and draft-order identifiers are returned. The CRM and operations revisions reviewed for this page use different API contracts; live end-to-end compatibility has not been verified.
Built on Frappe

The custom application uses Vue 3, frappe-ui, Python/Frappe, MariaDB and Redis. Frappe supplies the base CRM, administration and framework services. I added focused frontend and Python tests. I have not recorded current test pass counts or measured business improvements for this page.
problem: Sales staff needed one place to receive enquiries, call customers from the browser, obtain and revise quotations and hand confirmed business to operations, with each team seeing and changing only what its role allows.
challenges: Two call legs, events out of order
The staff member’s browser can connect even when the customer never answers, and the incoming call signal can arrive before the outbound API response.
Correlate the provider’s call identifier, buffer early invitations, separate uncertain dial results from failures and treat provider webhooks and scheduled reconciliation as the outcome authority.
More state-machine logic and provider-specific testing.
One phone per agent
Several tabs or stale registrations could ring multiple browser instances and interfere with call setup.
Web Locks keep one active softphone tab, with reconnect policies, generation guards, pinned SDK versions and targeted patches.
Web Locks do not coordinate separate browsers or machines, and the SDK patches need checking on every upgrade.
Sales stage and customer engagement
One status field cannot show both how far a sale has progressed and whether the customer has gone quiet.
Separate business stage and engagement state, enforce transitions in Python and connect call dispositions and follow-up retries to the model.
Two state dimensions must stay consistent across forms, APIs and automation.
limits: Built on Frappe CRM: the platform, administration, standard lists and framework services predate my work. Browser calling targets Chrome and Edge.
result: Enquiries, calls, quotations and the operations handoff live in linked records with enforced stage rules. A confirmed lead creates its operations project and draft order from the CRM, and a failed handoff stays retryable instead of looking complete.
context: 3 months of build, now in maintenance

Approximate total, supplied by me. A measure of the system's use, not of my contribution alone.

name: Project Visualization Library
indexSummary: A shared React package for project navigation and unit selection across two applications.

cover.alt: Illustration of a shared floor-and-unit grid connected to operations and customer views, with one unit selected.

summary: A reusable React package for navigating project hierarchies, reading unit progress and working with selected units. Used by the operations platform and a customer dashboard.
ownership: I created and primarily maintain the shared package and implemented its use across the two applications.
sections: Shared interface
The package provides hierarchical navigation, floor grids, status badges and filters, progress summaries, unit details, timelines, selectors and survey forms.
Application boundaries

Hosts supply data and callbacks and own authentication, APIs, persistence and business validation. The operations application owns offline storage and sync; the package supplies the reusable interface.
Rendering and distribution
The grid supports recursive hierarchy paths and virtualisation within expanded floors. The package builds ESM and CommonJS outputs with TypeScript declarations and supports React 18 and 19.
Late host data overrides restored selections

The selection panel filters restored selections against disabled units and repeats that pruning whenever the host’s disabled set changes. A unit selected before an availability request finishes is removed if the later response makes it ineligible.
images: Project totals and units grouped by floor, flat and room.
Component statuses, specifications and the selected unit’s location.
Survey and production history for the selected unit.

decision.label: Shared React package
decision.title: Share the UI, not the data layer.
decision.implementation: Typed props, callbacks and adapters connect the same visualization components to two applications.
decision.boundary: Each host owns its authentication, API access, persistence and business validation.

problem: Operations staff and customers need the same project and unit information for different jobs: staff select, survey and track units, while customers follow progress. Without a shared package, each application would build and maintain its own project-tracking interface.
challenges: Reliable photo uploads
A cancelled upload could resolve later and reappear, concurrent completions could drop images, and a form could submit before photo URLs existed.
Track local upload identities, ignore cancelled results, read current state on each completion and hold submission while uploads run.
Cancelling hides the result but cannot abort the request, because the host’s upload callback exposes no abort.
One interface, two hosts
The two applications use different routers, React versions and data layers.
Typed props, callbacks and a host-supplied fetcher. The package contains no router, API client or credentials, and React stays a peer dependency.
Each host writes adapters and orchestrates its own queries and actions.
Selections after an availability update
A restored selection could arrive before the host had finished loading which units are disabled.
Re-prune the selection whenever disabled units change, not only on the first render.
Selection state has to stay synchronised with inputs that change after mount.
facts: applications use the package
Verified through dependency declarations and imports in both.
test files
File count in the inspected revision. Not a test-case or coverage count.
limits: No authentication, database, persistence or offline queue. The package presents states supplied by its host, and the backend owns permissions and business rules. It is a data-driven progress view, not a 3D or CAD renderer.
result: The operations and customer applications render project hierarchies from one package instead of two separate implementations. It ships as versioned ESM and CommonJS builds with type declarations through a tag-triggered release workflow.
context: Sole developer for the initial build

demonstration.title: Try the two host views
demonstration.intro: Switch the host application, select a unit, then change its eligibility after selection. The shared view reacts to host inputs; each host keeps control of its data and rules.
demonstration.boundary: Illustrative grid with synthetic units, not the production package. Customer and operations views demonstrate different host configurations; these controls do not represent a permissions check.

labels.customerNote: The customer host supplies progress data and owns its own API access and routing.
labels.packageNote: Hierarchy, selection, detail panels and progress rendering live in the reusable package.
labels.backendNote: The backend checks permissions, stores confirmed records and enforces business rules.
labels.selectionNote: A selected unit can be rendered by the package while actions are handled by its host.

name: Public Brand Website & CMS
indexSummary: A server-rendered website with Strapi articles, enquiry forms connected to Frappe CRM and shared EC2 staging.

cover.alt: Illustration of editable article blocks becoming a published page, with a separate enquiry sent to the CRM.

summary: A public-facing SSR website, structured enquiry flows and a Strapi publishing platform, with staging deployment on AWS EC2.
ownership: I implemented the website and CMS together and set up their shared staging environment.
sections: Website and enquiries

Built multi-step homeowner and contractor enquiry forms, pincode lookup, Zod validation and server-side lead delivery. Migrated the CRM integration from Freshworks to Frappe while retaining form workflows and attribution data. The CRM determines duplicate-record outcomes.
Campaign attribution

First-touch and last-touch campaign parameters persist for 180 and 30 days, and supported ad click IDs travel with each enquiry, so campaign context survives when a visitor lands on one page and submits from another.
Content publishing

Configured and extended Strapi with article, author, category, site and SEO models, reusable content blocks and S3 media. The SSR website renders published content with search, filtering and pagination. Strapi provides the administration interface and core publishing functionality. The block renderer handles rich text, images, tables, information boxes, quotes, calls to action, FAQs and embedded video as distinct content types.
Staging operations

Set up separate website and CMS processes on one EC2 instance using PM2, Nginx hostname routing and HTTPS. Configured localhost-only PostgreSQL, IAM-based S3 access and daily compressed database backups with seven-day local retention.
images: Public website homepage with product introduction and consultation links.
Featured articles, categories, author information and article search.
Strapi’s entry editor showing the configured article fields, featured image and rich-text content block.
The corresponding sample article rendered on the public website.
The configured blog collection in Strapi’s content manager, using sample entries.
problem: The brand needed a product-discovery and enquiry channel that delivers structured leads to sales with their campaign context, and a way for editors to publish articles without a code release.
challenges: Different CRM responses
A submission can create a lead, match an existing one, reactivate it, reach a closed record or fail.

One server-side lead request recognises created, existing and reactivated leads as success, routes closed matches to a follow-up state, and maps validation, rate limits and service errors to failure states. Credentials stay on the server.
The website stays coupled to the CRM’s response contract.
Flexible articles, consistent pages
Editors need varied article layouts, while the site needs consistent, server-rendered pages.
Model the article body as reusable CMS blocks, each rendered by a dedicated React component.
Schema changes need matching renderer and type changes, and sometimes a content migration.
One small staging server
Run an SSR website and a CMS without mixing their origins or process configuration.
Separate hostnames and managed processes behind one Nginx, HTTPS on both, a database reachable only on localhost and S3 access through an instance role instead of stored keys.
Both applications share one instance’s memory, CPU and failure domain. It is not a highly available setup.
limits: Enquiry forms submit a lead; they do not book a calendar slot. Strapi provides the administration interface and publishing; I configured and extended it. The infrastructure described is shared staging.
result: Lead delivery moved from Freshworks to the company's Frappe CRM while keeping the website's form workflows and attribution payloads. Editors publish articles from Strapi without a code release.
context: Sole developer for the initial build
